rows.label: Share of the donations a meta charity's donors make that the charity caused (its own effect), when it has no donor survey of its own

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: Pledge counterfactuality coefficient 33% 26% ... Non-pledge counterfactual coefficient 28% 17%
source.note: Giving What We Can's donor surveys, the only published measurement of a meta charity's counterfactual influence on its donors' giving: best guesses 32.7% (pledgers) and 28.0% (other donors through its platform), conservative 26.0% and 17.0%; its 2023 pledger survey's estimate, 40.2%, which already counts non-respondents at half the respondents' influence (survey_nonrespondent_influence) (working sheet, 'Pledge counterfactuality coefficient'). Low: below the conservative non-pledge figure; high: above the survey's discounted 40.2% (its raw answer before the non-respondent step is 55%).

rows.explainer: Of the donations a meta charity records or channels (through its platform, by its pledgers, by people it advised), the share that happened only because of it: the rest its donors would have given to the same effective charities anyway. A meta model reads its own donor survey where it has one (an observed input with its source), otherwise this figure. A different question from the new-money share: of the donations the charity caused, how much would not have been given at all (new) and how much was redirected from other charities (shifted). 30%, from 15% to 45%.

rows.label: Share of new giving pledgers recording donations in their first pledge year

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: y₀ 59.4% 0.0076 7.90e-13 Initial percentage of pledgers recording donations
source.note: Exponential decay to a floor fitted to 10% Pledge cohorts 2017–2023 by years since pledging; range about two standard errors.

rows.explainer: Pledge persistence, part 1 of 3: of people who take a lifetime giving pledge, the share giving (recorded) in their first year. With the decay and the floor: share giving in year t = floor + (first year − floor) × (1 − decay)^t. The only published cohort data on how pledges hold up; every pledge model reads it unless the organisation publishes its own.

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: r 48.0% 0.0276 1.20e-07 Annual decay rate of the non-floor component
source.note: Range about two standard errors.

rows.explainer: Pledge persistence, part 2 of 3: each year the share of pledgers giving above the floor falls by about half.

rows.label: Long-term share of pledgers still giving (floor)

source.title: Giving What We Can, 2023–2024 Impact Evaluation (Aidan Whitfield, June 2025)
source.quote: c 27.8% 0.0076 3.55e-10 Long-term floor percentage of pledgers recording donations
source.note: Fitted on up to 10 years of data. Low: our judgment that the share may fall further after year 10 (the report: 'it is entirely possible that the percentage of reporting pledgers will drop again'); high: about two standard errors and a half.

rows.explainer: Pledge persistence, part 3 of 3: the share of pledgers who keep giving for good, about 28%. The report finds the decline levels off at 25–30% for older cohorts.

rows.label: Rethink Priorities' cross-cause research and surveys: share informing global health decisions (our judgment)
rows.explainer: Our judgment of the share of Rethink Priorities' worldview investigations and surveys work in 2025 (weighted by the two teams' expenses, $718,655 and $315,442) that informs global health decisions. No split is published; from the outputs its Form 990 lists: worldview investigations' AI risk-attitude work (AI safety), its AI consciousness model and digital minds estimate (no cause on the site), its human-animal trade-off and moral-weight work (animal welfare), the moral parliament tool and cause-prioritisation work (all three), and models of movement building (effective altruism, valued at the rest); surveys' Open Philanthropy surveys of LLM use and AI attitudes (AI), plant-based meat and wild animal welfare attitude studies (animal welfare), and Pulse and the community survey (effective altruism and giving). Global health gets the smallest share: little of the two teams' 2025 work is specific to it, beyond the cross-cause tools that include it.
